idiom_name: actor-isolated Set guard (or a unique-constraint claim)
implementation_notes: Swift's claim primitive is Set.insert, which returns (inserted: Bool, memberAfterInsert: Element): inserted == false means the key was already present. Wrapping the set in an actor serializes the check-and-claim without hand-written locks (a serial DispatchQueue serves the same role in pre-concurrency code), but the actor is process-local, so competing instances or restarts need a durable store instead - a SQLite/GRDB table with a UNIQUE idempotency key, or the broker's own duplicate detection. Set entries never expire, so retention must be swept explicitly.
pitfalls: Actor isolation covers one process only; a scaled-out consumer needs the durable claim, not a second actor.
Holding actor isolation across await applyEffects suspends every other claim - claim, leave the actor, then process.
A Set has no TTL; a long-running receiver must prune by timestamp or move keys into a store with expiry.
